questions.q: According to this lesson's decision framework, what should always happen before reaching for Numba, Cython, or multiprocessing?
options: Rewriting the entire codebase in a different language
Profiling to find the actual bottleneck, rather than guessing which part of the code is slow
Installing every available performance library just in case
Switching from pandas to polars
questions.explain: The chapter's checklist starts with profiling (cProfile/line_profiler) because intuition about what's slow is unreliable -- optimizing the wrong part wastes effort with no payoff.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a compiled O(n^2) loop (e.g. via Numba) 'is still O(n^2)'?
options: Because Numba doesn't actually compile anything

Because compiling the implementation reduces the constant factor but does not change the algorithm's underlying growth rate -- if the real problem is a complexity issue, a faster implementation of the same algorithm won't fix it at large enough scale
Because O(n^2) algorithms can never be compiled
Because Numba always produces incorrect results for O(n^2) algorithms
questions.explain: Lesson 13 distinguished constant-factor problems from complexity problems; compiling a loop (Numba/Cython) addresses the constant factor, not the growth rate, so an algorithm that scales badly will still eventually become too slow as data grows, no matter how compiled it is.

questions.q: What is the recommended rough order of effort-vs-payoff for speeding up Python numerical code, per this lesson?
options: Cython, then multiprocessing, then Numba, then vectorization
Vectorize, then Numba, then multiprocessing, then Cython, then (rarely) rewrite in another language/service
Multiprocessing first always, since more cores is always better
Rewrite in another language immediately, skipping all Python-level optimization
questions.explain: The lesson lays out vectorization first (lowest effort, broad applicability), then Numba, then multiprocessing for independent chunked work, then Cython for cases Numba can't handle, and a full rewrite only as a last resort.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which situation is NOT, by itself, a good reason to optimize slow code?
options: The code runs in a production pipeline every night
The code sits in a latency-sensitive path responding to a live trading signal
A one-off research script takes three minutes to run once, and the result is then read and the script is not run again
The function is called millions of times and is now blocking other work
questions.explain: A one-off script run once, where the runtime doesn't block anything else, is a correct use of time, not a performance problem -- the lesson explicitly distinguishes this from code that runs repeatedly or is latency-sensitive.

questions.q: Why do none of this chapter's tools (profiling, Numba, Cython, multiprocessing) help an I/O-bound script that is slow because it's waiting on a database query?
options: Because I/O-bound code is always a Big-O problem
Because the bottleneck is waiting on an external resource, not CPU computation, so CPU-focused tools like Numba or multiprocessing don't address the actual cause of the delay
Because I/O-bound code cannot be profiled with cProfile
Because database queries always run in O(n^2) time
questions.explain: This chapter's tools target CPU-bound work; an I/O-bound bottleneck (waiting on network/disk) needs a different kind of fix (reducing round trips, caching, async I/O), which is outside this chapter's scope.
